newsitem.title: USA: Intel to pass on MMX savings to PC makers.
newsitem.headline: Intel to pass on MMX savings to PC makers.

text.p: Intel Corp. said Thursday it has begun distributing third quarter price lists to customers, and will pass along savings from manufacturing efficiencies on its MMX-based processors to PC makers.
One source familiar with the price list said prices ranged in the "ballpark" from unchanged to roughly 50 percent lower.

Overall, an Intel spokesmen said the third quarter price lists will contain a range of price reductions on its microprocessors similar to those it has offered in its past regular quarterly price changes. Intel declined to provide details on prices until the changes take effect in late July.

The level of Intel's regular price reductions, which occur three times a year for consumer-end microprocessors and every quarter for its higher-end chips, is a closely watched barometer of the health of the overall PC market.

Intel, the world's largest semiconductor maker and a bellwether for the technology sector, spooked Wall Street just two weeks ago with its statement that it expected second quarter results to fall below analysts expectations.
But the company also said, at the same time, that it was experiencing strong demand for its latest products, including the Pentium II microprocessor formally introduced last month.

While price changes historically vary from chip to chip due to Intel's view of their position in the market and any competitive offerings, its pricing plans this time will aim to address the demand for chips incorporating its MMX mulitimedia technology, including the new Pentium II products.

"The market is rapidly moving to MMX technology enabled processors and we are doing everything we can to accomodate that move and to supply what customers would like to buy," Intel spokesman Howard High said.

High said Intel has been able to gain "about 10 percent upside in our manufacturing efficiency" by shrinking the size of its Pentium with MMX processor, enabling it to produce more on each silicon wafer it makes.

"That gets more chips out, that lowers your cost and increases your supply that you can provide....We continue to share those (cost) improvements with customers," he said. "We are adjusting our product mix in order to satisfy demand."
Intel recently told analysts that it expects its newly launched Pentium II processors to account for roughly half its productg mix by the middle of 1998.

Intel shares traded as low as 142, off 5-1/2, Thursday morning after a Goldman Sachs analyst cut his 1997 earnings estimates and a Cowen & Co analyst downgraded Intel to a neutral rating from a "buy" recommendation.
The shares were off 3-5/8 at 143-7/8 in early afternoon trade.

Worries persist over whether Intel's remarks over the past two weeks about weaker than expected demand, especially in Europe, signal a broader slowdown in the PC sector just as the company has refreshed its product line.
On Wednesday, online news service ZDNet News reported Intel would cut its prices on Pentium MMX chips by up to 50 percent.

ZDNet, citing sources close to Intel, said for example the price of Intel's 200 megahertz (MHz) Pentium MMX for volumes above 1,000 procesors would be slashed in the third quarter by roughly 50 percent, to $247 from $492, while the 166 MHz would be cut to $142 from $270, and the 233 MHz, introduced just last week, to $378 from $594.
Low-powered notebook chips would fall in price to $341 from $508 on the 166 MHz and to $236 from $336 on the 150 MHz. it said.
Intel declined to discuss specific price changes until they take effect on July 28. Specific prices may vary slightly by customer depending on volumes and other contractual terms.
